title: Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers § 46: Documents Relating to a Representation
author: American Law Institute

dom.t: Document stewardship: Digital files preserve professional duties

st.t: Document stewardship: Digital files preserve professional duties
st.an: Restatement § 46 directly supports the cluster’s proposition that document stewardship imposes continuing duties of safeguarding, client access and timely delivery. It also supports the cluster’s distinction between broad inspection rights and delivery of documents the client reasonably needs, subject to specified exceptions.
qs: Documents Relating to a Representation  (1) A lawyer must take reasonable steps to safeguard documents in the lawyer's possession relating to the representation of a client or former client.
(2) On request, a lawyer must allow a client or former client to inspect and copy any document possessed by the lawyer relating to the representation, unless substantial grounds exist to refuse.

mo.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
Digital ethics: Existing duties extend to new media
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Technology competence: Delegation preserves professional responsibility

kp.k: Lawyers must reasonably safeguard representation documents
kp.d: Section 46(1) states a duty to take reasonable steps to safeguard documents held by a lawyer relating to current or former client representations. This is a professional-duty statement, not an empirical finding or an AI-specific claim.
qs: (1) A lawyer must take reasonable steps to safeguard documents in the lawyer's possession relating to the representation of a client or former client.

kp.k: Clients have qualified rights to inspect and copy documents
kp.d: Section 46(2) requires lawyers, on request, to permit current and former clients to inspect and copy any possessed document relating to the representation, unless substantial grounds justify refusal.
qs: (2) On request, a lawyer must allow a client or former client to inspect and copy any document possessed by the lawyer relating to the representation, unless substantial grounds exist to refuse.

kp.k: Reasonably needed documents must be delivered promptly
kp.d: Section 46(3) requires delivery of originals and copies of other representation documents that clients or former clients reasonably need, at an appropriate time and in any event promptly after the representation ends. Client consent to nondelivery or substantial grounds for refusing delivery qualify this obligation.
qs: (3) Unless a client or former client consents to nondelivery or substantial grounds exist for refusing to make delivery, a lawyer must deliver to the client or former client, at an appropriate time and in any event promptly after the representation ends, such originals and copies of other documents possessed by the lawyer relating to the representation as the client or former client reasonably needs.

kp.k: A retention exception further limits document delivery rights
kp.d: Section 46(4) permits refusal to deliver originals or copies in circumstances allowed by § 43(1), notwithstanding subsections (2) and (3). The document's corpus-placement commentary characterizes this exception as the lawyer's retention interest and cautions that access rights are not unconditional; the text of § 43(1) is not supplied.
qs: (4) Notwithstanding Subsections (2) and (3), a lawyer may decline to deliver to a client or former client an original or copy of any document under circumstances permitted by § 43(1).
The § 43(1) carve-out in § 46(4) is the lawyer's retention interest, and it is the reason the access right cannot be read as unconditional.

kp.k: File access rights do not establish clean ownership title
kp.d: The corpus-placement commentary reports that ABA Formal Opinion 471 (2015) identifies these provisions as advocating the majority entire-file approach. It uses § 46 as a framework for client-matter-data analysis, emphasizing fiduciary-grounded entitlement and access rather than a clean property-ownership title. The document does not itself claim that AI changes these rights.
qs: These provisions are the standing black-letter statement of the client's file rights that ABA Formal Opinion 471 (2015) identifies as advocating the majority "entire file" approach.

In the client-matter-data-ownership analysis, § 46 supports the claim that clients hold strong, rule-based rights of access in the matter file — framed as entitlement and access grounded in fiduciary protection rather than as a clean property-ownership title.
